Machine Learning.title: Why Linear Models Can Still Work in a Complex and Changing World
Machine Learning.summary: Linear models can predict well in complex domains even when underlying mechanisms are nonlinear. We argue that this can occur because the complexity of the world exceeds the complexity that can be learned reliably from finite, partially observed data. Flexible models can exploit curvature, thresholds, and interactions that fit one hospital, period, population, policy setting, or measurement process but fail elsewhere. When this instability lies mainly in the nonlinear component, omitting it can give linear models lower prediction error in a new environment. We connect this claim to work on simple linear rules, bias and variance, regularization, best linear prediction, measurement error, distribution shift, invariance, Rashomon sets, and underspecification. Proposition 1 gives a simple squared-error case in which a nonlinear rule learned in the training environment raises target error because it transfers too weakly; finite-sample estimation error can strengthen this result. Partial observation alone is not enough: the link between observed variables and unobserved factors must vary across environments. Stable nonlinear structure favors flexible models, and linear models remain vulnerable to linear spurious relationships. Model complexity should therefore be chosen by cross-environment stability as well as training-data accuracy.

Machine Learning.title: Model-free Bayesian Clustering and Multimodal Posterior Summarisation
Machine Learning.summary: We develop a model-free, noise-aware Bayesian clustering framework that constructs a martingale posterior over clusterings from a predictive Bayesian perspective. This avoids explicit likelihood-prior model specification, expensive MCMC sampling, and mode-seeking variational approximations, while accommodating irregular cluster shapes and enabling parallel generation of posterior draws. To interpret the posterior over high-dimensional, noise-aware clusterings, we introduce a Wasserstein-type summarization method. Using a novel noise-aware loss, this approach compresses the large collection of posterior draws into a small set of weighted representatives, capturing distinct cluster structures and noise assignments. Further, we marginalise the uncertainty in the density level, avoiding reliance on a specific choice. We establish theoretical properties of the proposed loss and guarantees for the level-marginal posterior approximation. Results demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in capturing clustering and noise uncertainty.

Machine Learning.title: PlacePulse: Learning Transferable Place Representations from Structural Geographic Data
Machine Learning.summary: Geospatial machine learning often depends on task-specific feature engineering over large collections of sociodemographic, business, and environmental variables. Geospatial foundation models offer reusable representations of place, but leading approaches typically encode dynamic signals, such as mobility and search activity, or visual signals from satellite imagery. Few models represent the static structural composition of places (who lives and works there, which businesses operate there, and which risks they face) as transferable embeddings at fine spatial resolution. We introduce PlacePulse, a structural geospatial foundation model that compresses 572 attributes, expanded to 2,288 inputs through H3 neighborhood aggregates, into 256-dimensional unit-norm embeddings for 1,055,537 H3 resolution-7 cells in the United States. We also introduce a reusable two-axis benchmark that separates intrinsic representation quality from downstream predictive utility across multiple targets and spatial supports. Intrinsically, the embeddings reconstruct standardized inputs with mean $R^2 = 0.853$, use 251 of 256 approximately decorrelated dimensions, and show strong spatial organization, with Moran's $I = 0.93$ on the leading principal component and autocorrelation persisting beyond the input radius. Extrinsically, across 74 held-out targets from 12 external sources and four spatial supports, PlacePulse outperforms a dimensionality-matched feature-selection baseline on targets unrelated to the training inputs and is competitive with Google's Population Dynamics Foundation Model, leading on health, economic, election, economic-mobility and social-vulnerability outcomes, with relative strengths that vary by domain. These findings position structural composition as a distinct and complementary modality for geospatial foundation models, not simply a fallback where behavioral or imagery data are unavailable.

Machine Learning.title: Understanding Transformer-based Vision Models through Inversion
Machine Learning.summary: Understanding the internal mechanisms of deep neural networks remains a central challenge in machine learning. In computer vision, one promising yet only preliminarily explored approach is feature inversion via inverse networks, which reconstructs images from intermediate representations using trained inverse networks. In this study, we revisit feature inversion via inverse networks, introducing a novel, modular variant that enables a computationally more efficient application of the technique while, in some cases, producing semantically more coherent image reconstructions. We apply our method to large-scale transformer-based vision models, specifically Detection Transformer, Vision Transformer, Swin Transformer, and Data-Efficient Image Transformer, analyzing the resulting reconstructions across network depth. Our main analysis compares Detection Transformer and Vision Transformer, which exhibit the most informative differences among the evaluated architectures. At the same time, results for Swin Transformer and Data-Efficient Image Transformer support the broader applicability of our framework. Our findings reveal gradual representational changes across transformer layers as a shared characteristic of Detection Transformer and Vision Transformer, as well as systematic differences in how they preserve contextual shape and fine-grained image details, and in their robustness to color perturbations. These findings deepen understanding of transformer-based vision models and demonstrate the utility of modular feature inversion as an interpretability tool.

Machine Learning.title: BLOKS: Scaling Kernel Solvers with Sketched Block Preconditioning
Machine Learning.summary: Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR) is a theoretically sound algorithm for nonparametric learning, which is also often used to investigate properties of deep learning. However, the exact KRR formulation incurs time and memory costs preventing applicability to large datasets, motivating the development of approximate solvers. These algorithms rely on (i) iterative methods, to avoid the computational burden of direct solutions; (ii) sketching or batching, to reduce the problem size; and (iii) preconditioning, to accelerate convergence. While crucial for fast convergence, preconditioning incurs memory costs that can be managed by lowering the number of free parameters of the model, potentially at the expense of expressivity and hence accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose BLOKS, a Conjugate Gradient-based solver for Nyström-sketched KRR built around a novel preconditioner that combines a block Jacobi approximation with sketching. The BLOKS preconditioner has memory cost independent of both the dataset size and the number of parameters, allowing scaling to large models. We provide a memory-efficient, GPU-accelerated implementation and show that BLOKS achieves excellent accuracy while retaining favorable time/memory complexity. Indeed, on standard large-scale datasets used to benchmark kernel solvers, BLOKS achieves comparable or better performances than state-of-the-art methods.

Machine Learning.title: Enhancing Tabular Learners with Context-Aware Semantic Embeddings
Machine Learning.summary: While modern tabular learners excel at capturing statistical patterns, they frequently operate in a semantic vacuum, treating textual features as discrete symbols, ignoring the rich semantics inherent in feature names or cell entries. We propose CASE (Context-Aware Semantic Embeddings), a novel framework that bridges the gap between the semantic understanding of Large Language Models (LLMs) and the statistical capabilities of tabular learners. Unlike existing methods that embed rows in isolation, CASE utilizes a contextualization strategy: we pre-fill the KV cache of a custom-trained Gemma 3-based Tabular Language Model with a representative sample of rows to establish a persistent anchor of the dataset's semantics. This ensures that generated row embeddings are dynamically contextualized, resolving semantic ambiguities and anchoring representations in domain-specific context. Our experiments across several benchmarks (CARTE, TextTab, and TabArena) demonstrate that CASE substantially improves the performance of tabular learners on semantically rich datasets, particularly in low-data regimes.

Machine Learning.title: asdex: Automatic Sparse Differentiation in JAX
Machine Learning.summary: Many tasks in scientific computing and machine learning require the Jacobian or Hessian matrix of a function. Automatic differentiation (AD) computes these derivatives to machine precision, but materializing a dense $m \times n$ Jacobian requires $n$ forward-mode or $m$ reverse-mode AD passes, one per column or row. For a large class of functions, each output depends on only a few inputs, making the derivative matrix sparse. Automatic sparse differentiation (ASD) exploits this structure in four steps: detection of the input-agnostic sparsity pattern, coloring of a graph to group columns or rows that can share an AD pass, compressed differentiation to compute a compressed derivative matrix with one AD pass per color, and finally decompression into the original sparsity pattern. The number of colors, and hence of AD passes, is often independent of the problem dimension: a banded Jacobian with $b$ contiguous bands, for instance, only ever requires $b$ colors, regardless of its size. asdex offers the first standalone ASD toolkit in the popular JAX ecosystem. With $\texttt{asdex.jacobian}$ and $\texttt{asdex.hessian}$, it provides sparse drop-in replacements for $\texttt{jax.jacobian}$ and $\texttt{jax.hessian}$.

Machine Learning.title: Overcoming Data Imbalances with Expert Selection Biases
Machine Learning.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become the standard architecture for frontier LLMs. The multiple parallel experts in each transformer block theoretically enable expert specialization according to categories such as domains, languages, or modalities during pretraining. However, when data is imbalanced across categories, minority categories can become concentrated in a small fraction of the expert pool or spread inefficiently across them, effectively limiting their available capacity. In this work, we demonstrate that category-conditioned expert-selection biases can preferentially route tokens from different categories toward specialized expert pools. By applying biases based on input category, we provide a simple way to induce soft category-aligned specialization. This intervention encourages categories toward distinct expert subsets while retaining cross-category sharing when useful. More importantly, it enables the over-allocation of expert capacity to categories that would otherwise be disadvantaged by data scarcity. We observe performance improvements across modalities, low-resource languages, and code in models up to 10.6B parameters. At our smallest and largest model scales, these gains are equivalent to allocating 18.5% and 2.7% additional baseline training tokens, respectively. Overall, our results show that expert biases can serve as a lightweight control for category-level expert allocation, making room for low-resource categories while retaining standard MoE inference.

Image and Video Processing.title: A Miniaturized Wi-Fi HaLow-Based Wireless Imaging Transfer System for Capsule Endoscopy
Image and Video Processing.summary:
Wireless capsule endoscopy is constrained by severe limitations in size, available power, and reliable data transmission through biological tissues. Although recent advances in miniature imaging sensors have improved image quality, the wireless transmission of color images at practical frame rates remains a challenging task under the tight capsule constraints.
  We present the design and the experimental validation of a miniaturized Wireless Imaging Transfer (WIT) system for capsule endoscopy based on a sub-GHz IEEE 802.11ah (Wi-Fi HaLow) wireless link. In addition, a preliminary in-vivo validation of Wi-Fi HaLow communication is reported, showing that a stable through-body wireless link can be established across biological tissues in a clinically relevant porcine model. These in-vivo results provide direct experimental support for the adoption of sub-GHz Wi-Fi HaLow for capsule endoscopy applications.
  Experimental results demonstrate stable wireless image transmission at a resolution of 320x320 pixels, with measured end-to-end data rates above 12 Mbps and a transmission energy efficiency of 20.7 nJ/bit. We also report a detailed power consumption analysis, with a breakdown of the contributions from the imaging sensor, illumination, digital processing, and RF transmission. When all active subsystem contributions are considered, including the camera, digital processing, RF transmission, and illumination at 60% LED brightness, the total power consumption is approximately 477 mW, corresponding to a complete-chain energy consumption of approximately 39.6 nJ/bit. Overall, the measured performance confirms that sub-GHz Wi-Fi HaLow provides a promising trade-off among throughput, robustness, and energy efficiency for wireless imaging in capsule endoscopy.

Image and Video Processing.title: Can Multimodal Decision Models Classify Breast Ultrasound Images? Benchmarking CLEF and CLEF-Flash Across Prompts and Datasets
Image and Video Processing.summary: Multimodal decision models return probabilities over predefined alternatives, offering a structured interface for image classification. This study benchmarks inference with CLEF and CLEF-Flash on 2818 breast ultrasound images from Dataset B, BUSI, and BUS-BRA. Dataset B and BUS-BRA use binary benign-malignant classification, whereas BUSI includes normal, benign, and malignant categories. Model parameters remain unchanged, and original images are submitted without user-defined preprocessing. Three prompts provide minimal labels, an explicit classification task, or sonographic criteria. We report accuracy, macro F1, balanced accuracy, macro precision, throughput, and latency. CLEF-Flash with the clinical prompt achieves the highest accuracy on all three datasets: 74.85% on Dataset B, 66.28% on BUSI, and 51.63% on BUS-BRA. On BUSI, however, CLEF with the task-guided prompt achieves the highest macro F1 (64.51%) and balanced accuracy (68.72%). CLEF-Flash has lower latency in every matched comparison. Clinical instructions improve CLEF-Flash accuracy relative to the minimal prompt but reduce CLEF accuracy on all datasets. Confusion matrices reveal frequent benign-to-malignant errors, particularly on BUS-BRA, where all configurations fall below the 67.63% accuracy of a majority-class predictor. These findings demonstrate dataset-and prompt-dependent performance and motivate class-specific evaluation before applying multimodal decision models to breast ultrasound analysis.

Image and Video Processing.title: Model-agnostic Knowledge Augmented Machine Learning for Weakly Annotated Bioimaging Data
Image and Video Processing.summary: Machine learning models are increasingly used for automated feature extraction from weakly annotated bioimaging data, such as microscopy and cytomorphology images. Due to the sole dependency of automated feature extraction, existing methods yield inconsistent classification performance across weakly annotated datasets. Here, we propose a model-agnostic knowledge augmentation method that enables ML models to exploit domain knowledge beyond what automated feature extraction can capture. The proposed approach improves classification performance across seven ML architectures. When integrated with masked autoencoder-based self-supervised learning, our method achieves the strongest overall performance, improving precision by 2.9% over the next-best method on three in-house microscopy datasets and by an average of 6.8% across three public cytomorphology benchmarks. We perform nucleus-level classification based on mislocalization of TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, a phenotype linked to Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), using three independent microscopy datasets of motor neurons derived from human induced pluripotent stem cells. Accurate quantification of this phenotype at scale remains challenging and may contribute to inconsistencies across studies. Application of the best-performing model to these microscopy datasets reveals biological interpretations related to ALS, including dose-dependent effects of the proteasomal stressor, MG132, and the oxidative stressor, sodium arsenite (SA), on TDP-43 mislocalization, variable pathology in motor neurons from sporadic and familial ALS donors, and a lack of protection of the pharmacological compounds, edaravone and niclosamide, against SA-induced TDP-43 mislocalization. Together, our pipeline enables in-vitro cellular image analysis to advance understanding of ALS-associated pathology and potential treatments.

Image and Video Processing.title: Radiomics-Based Thyroid Nodule Classification with Label-Conditional Conformal Prediction
Image and Video Processing.summary: Thyroid nodule malignancy assessment relies on ultrasound imaging, yet current risk stratification systems suffer from substantial interobserver variability, contributing to a high rate of unnecessary biopsies. We propose a radiomics-based framework combining quantitative feature extraction via PyRadiomics with a Generalized Additive Model (GAM) classifier, selected among six candidates for its favorable trade-off between discriminative performance and interpretability. To complement point predictions with uncertainty estimates, Cross-Conformal Prediction with label-conditional guarantees is applied, flagging ambiguous cases for clinical review rather than forcing a binary decision. Experiments are conducted on TN5000, a publicly available ultrasound dataset of thyroid nodules. After Spearman correlation filtering, 36 features are retained and the GAM achieves an AUC of $0.89$, a sensitivity of $0.83$, and a specificity of $0.82$ on the validation set. At a significance level $ε=0.09$, selected to ensure empirical coverage guarantees on both classes, 63\% of nodules on the test set receive a certain (i.e., single-label) prediction, with conditional precision of $0.94$ for certain malignant and conditional Negative Predictive Value (NPV) of $0.73$ for certain benign cases, while the remaining 37\% are referred to the clinician.

Image and Video Processing.title: Leveraging Motion Estimation for Efficient Bayer-Domain Video Convolutional Networks
Image and Video Processing.summary: Existing computer vision pipelines suffer from two efficiency bottlenecks: image signal processors (ISPs) first convert Bayer pixel data to RGB pixel by pixel, and video models repeatedly process temporally redundant frames, leading to high power consumption and latency. In this paper, we propose a novel framework that eliminates the ISP and leverages motion estimation to accelerate video vision tasks directly in the Bayer domain. We introduce Motion Estimation-based Video Convolution (MEVC), which integrates sliding-window motion estimation into each convolutional layer, enabling prediction and residual-based refinement that reduces redundant computations across frames. This design bridges the structural gap between block-based motion estimation and spatial convolution, enabling accurate, low-cost processing. Our end-to-end pipeline supports raw Bayer input and achieves over 70% reduction in FLOPs with minimal accuracy degradation across video semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and object detection benchmarks, using both synthetic Bayer-converted and real Bayer video datasets.

Image and Video Processing.title: Selective Depthwise Separable Convolution for Lightweight Joint Source-Channel Coding in Wireless Image Transmission
Image and Video Processing.summary: Depthwise separable convolutional (DSConv) layers have been successfully applied to deep learning (DL)-based joint source-channel coding (JSCC) schemes to reduce computational complexity. However, a systematic investigation of the layerwise and ratio-wise replacement of standard convolutional (Conv) layers with DSConv layers in JSCC systems for wireless image transmission remains largely unexplored. In this letter, we propose a configurable lightweight JSCC framework that incorporates a selective replacement strategy, enabling flexible Conv-to-DSConv replacement at different replacement ratios and positions. By varying the replacement ratio, we obtain models with different computational complexities and analyze their impact on reconstruction performance. Furthermore, we investigate how replacements at different encoder and decoder depths influence reconstruction quality under a fixed replacement ratio. Our results show that Conv-to-DSConv replacement at the intermediate layers of the encoder and decoder achieves a favorable complexity-performance trade-off, revealing layer-wise redundancy in DL-based JSCC systems. Extensive experiments further demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves substantial parameter reduction with only slight performance degradation, enabling flexible complexity-performance trade-offs for resource-constrained edge devices.

Image and Video Processing.title: The Predictability Bias of Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning in Medical Imaging
Image and Video Processing.summary: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn by predicting teacher representations of masked regions from visible context. Point prediction summarizes the conditional target distribution and cannot reproduce variation that the context does not resolve. We call this constraint predictability bias. In computed tomography (CT), recurrent anatomy is predictable from context, whereas the sporadic, localized pathology that determines clinical interpretation often is not. We introduce TAP-JEPA, a ViT-B/3D trained on 113,611 CT volumes that is competitive with state-of-the-art encoders (COLIPRI, Merlin, VoxelFM) in scan-level classification. We then audit the learned predictive pathway by replaying the exact masking, teacher, and predictor computations used during training. Prediction lowers the mean Skill (prevalence-normalized average precision) from 0.388 to 0.271 for pathology, but only from 0.921 to 0.873 for anatomy. Along the teacher direction, separating pathology from matched control regions in the same organ, prediction moves pathology 34.7% toward the controls and controls 13.6% toward pathology, with larger shifts farther from visible context. Replacing visible matched-control representations increases surrounding-target prediction loss more than fully replacing pathology representations across four pathology categories. Downstream, removing all final-layer pathology tokens reduces the decision margin by at most 0.45% in four of seven scan-level probes. Together, these results show that contextual predictability is not a sufficient proxy for clinical relevance in medical representation learning. Training objectives should therefore retain diagnostic features regardless of their predictability from surrounding anatomy.

Image and Video Processing.title: Stochastic Finite-Transition Learning and Exploration for Accelerated MRI Reconstruction
Image and Video Processing.summary: Generative MRI reconstruction maps an initial source distribution to the target image distribution along a learned recovery trajectory. Common generative methods, such as diffusion and flow, typically learn fine-grained local dynamics whose integration defines this global mapping, hence requiring many network evaluations at inference. Existing few-step sampling approaches can lower computational burden by approximating large transformations from local dynamics, albeit at the expense of reconstruction fidelity. FLEX-MRI instead partitions recovery into a small number of finite intervals between retained states defined by progressive changes in k-space support, and directly learns the reconstruction change across each interval. Because such finite transitions can admit multiple plausible outcomes, FLEX-MRI combines support-relaxed finite-transition learning with stochastic exploration. During training, randomized k-space sampling masks define finite-transition targets with varying support, while the prediction loss remains unrestricted by each individual mask. At inference, FLEX-MRI perturbs a random subset of currently estimated k-space coefficients, allowing the learned predictor to stochastically explore alternative transition paths. Each predicted state is then reconciled with the acquired measurements through data consistency. We theoretically show that this stochastic exploration induces nonzero transition-level variation through the learned recovery map and data consistency without requiring an auxiliary generative sampler. Experiments on multi-coil MRI datasets show that FLEX-MRI outperforms competing methods while maintaining computational efficiency comparable to few-step baselines.

Image and Video Processing.title: One-Bin Fourier Challenges for Dimension-Free Reconstruction Certification
Image and Video Processing.summary: Partial-Fourier measurement underlies computational imaging, and its reconstructions increasingly come from iterative or learned solvers whose recovery guarantees are conditional on a signal model, a sampling law, and solver accuracy. None of those guarantees transfers to a particular committed output: it can satisfy every acquired coefficient while remaining badly wrong in the unmeasured nullspace. Native Fourier holdout does not repair this, since a spectrally concentrated error is missed unless its bin is drawn, so uniform worst-case risk needs a number of hidden bins proportional to the dimension. We propose a post-commit acceptance test: secret finite-phase masks turn one fixed Fourier readout into dense randomized residual checks, and a median-of-means threshold handles calibrated readout noise. We prove that errors above $E_{\rm rej}$ are rejected and errors below $E_{\rm acc}$ are accepted with confidence $1-δ$ once $q\ge C(1+Nσ^2/E_{\rm rej})^2\log(1/δ)$, explicitly exposing the one-bin resolution floor $Nσ^2/\sqrt q$; in the zero-noise limit, QPSK gives $4^{-q}$ soundness versus $97.9\%$ minimax false acceptance for a worst-case ordinary-bin error. At a fixed noise-to-threshold ratio, measured screening false acceptance fell from about $21\%$ at 16 checks to $5\%$ at 64; a data-consistent learned nullspace failure with NMSE $0.200$ was rejected by $96.9\%$ of challenge banks while 16 ordinary bins missed it $98.9\%$ of the time; and error statistics at 16 checks stayed stable from 128 through $65{,}536$ dimensions. The test supports solver acceptance, model selection, and stopping certification, with a certified fresh-bank error interval.

The certification procedure requires complex-valued linear Fourier measurements, whereas intensity-only acquisition does not directly provide them. The manuscript does not establish the additional acquisition procedure needed to bridge this gap

Image and Video Processing.title: Low, High, and Semantic-Level Vision-Language Learning for AI-Generated Image Detection
Image and Video Processing.summary: Driven by advances in diffusion models and autoregressive models, the fidelity and resolution of AI-generated images now rival those of real images. However, existing AI-generated image detection methods often downsample the images,inevitably overlooking critical low-level texture details in high-resolution AI-generated images, thereby limiting their detection performance. In addition, the continuous emergence of unknown generative models makes large-scale pre-training datasets inaccessible. To address these challenges, we propose a novel AI-generated image detector, termed LHSDet (Low-, High-, and Semantic-level Detection). Specifically, we formulate the AI-generated image detection task as a Visual Question Answering problem, leveraging a fine-tuned vision-language framework to fully exploit the complementary information between visual and textual modalities. Recognizing that the default visual encoder of existing vision-language models is not tailored for AI-generated image detection, we redesign a visual encoder to better capture both the low-level and high-level artifacts inherent in AI-generated images. Furthermore, we incorporate a semantic-level textual branch to enable multi-modal feature fusion and detection. Consequently, LHSDet employs a triple-branch architecture to extract complementary multi-modal features: a low-level visual branch that aggregates non-overlapping patches for local texture cues, a high-level visual branch based on SigLIP2 for global perception feature extraction,and a semantic-level textual branch that generates captions using BLIP-2. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that LHSDet achieves strong detection accuracy and robust performance across diverse generative models.

Image and Video Processing.title: Compression Hurts, Pooling Helps: Information Loss in Rayleigh-Scale Estimation from B-Mode Ultrasound
Image and Video Processing.summary: Clinical B-mode images are widely available as potential data sources for quantitative ultrasound (QUS) analysis for tissue characterization. However, standard clinical ultrasound devices apply unknown log-compression to RF envelope data before display and storage. Previous work has demonstrated estimation of the underlying RF envelope statistics in the presence of an unknown compression law. Using Fisher information analysis, we show that finite-offset log compression causes severe information loss when estimating the Rayleigh scale $σ$, which controls diffuse speckle. For a single image window, unknown compression raises the minimum achievable variance for unbiased estimation of $σ$ by a compression-independent factor of approximately 34.98. When $M$ equal-sized windows share the same unknown compression settings, the excess variance decays as $1/M$; even in the most favorable regime, reducing the variance inflation factor below 1.1 requires 340 windows. Our analysis treats the contrast parameter $a$ as unknown and the boundary offset $b$ as known; estimating $b$ experimentally shows even larger variance. We validate this theory using synthetic estimation experiments and demonstrate RF-scale recovery on real RF-envelope windows from the OASBUD dataset. Together, these results clarify the limitations of using routine B-mode images for QUS.

Image and Video Processing.title: Scale-specific auxiliary multi-task contrastive learning for deep liver vessel segmentation
Image and Video Processing.summary: Extracting hepatic vessels from abdominal images is of high interest for clinicians since it allows to divide the liver into functionally-independent Couinaud segments. In this respect, an automated liver blood vessel extraction is widely summoned. Despite the significant growth in performance of semantic segmentation methodologies, preserving the complex multi-scale geometry of main vessels and ramifications remains a major challenge. This paper provides a new deep supervised approach for vessel segmentation, with a strong focus on representations arising from the different scales inherent to the vascular tree geometry. In particular, we propose a new clustering technique to decompose the tree into various scale levels, from tiny to large vessels. Then, we extend standard 3D UNet to multi-task learning by incorporating scale-specific auxiliary tasks and contrastive learning to encourage the discrimination between scales in the shared representation. Promising results, depicted in several evaluation metrics, are revealed on the public 3D-IRCADb dataset.

Image and Video Processing.title: Multiclass histogram-based thresholding using kernel density estimation and scale-space representations
Image and Video Processing.summary: We present a method for multiclass thresholding of histograms whose modes may overlap so strongly that they merge into a unimodal distribution. The histogram is approximated by a nonparametric kernel density (KD) estimate, a mixture of Gaussians with one component per bin and a common bandwidth, whose parameters are determined by Expectation-Maximization (EM) iterations. Because the estimate is a Gaussian mixture, the semigroup property of Gaussian convolution yields its scale-space representation in closed form, at bandwidths both larger and smaller than the fitted one. The algorithm increases or decreases the bandwidth until the number of local minima of the estimate equals the number of requested classes minus one, and returns the positions of those minima as the threshold values. We validate the method on synthetic histograms with known thresholds, and we apply it to the histogram of X-ray computed tomography images of a natural porous sample in which the three phases strongly overlap. The porosity computed from the resulting segmentation agrees with the direct experimental measurement to within 4%, whereas K-means clustering misestimates it by 52%.

Image and Video Processing.title: Beyond Gate Weights: Decision-Level Interpretation of Radiomics-Image Feature Fusion for RCC Classification
Image and Video Processing.summary: Gate coefficients describe how a fusion layer weights intermediate features, but they do not necessarily reflect the magnitude of branch contributions at the classifier output. We investigate this distinction in a fixed 3D MedVAE--radiomics model for clear cell versus non-clear cell renal cell carcinoma classification from contrast-enhanced CT. Because the model uses a linear classification head, the binary decision logit can be decomposed exactly into a gated image term, a direct radiomics term, and a bias. We define effective radiomics dominance as the direct radiomics term's share of the summed absolute non-bias branch contributions and compare it with structural radiomics weighting. Internally, mean structural radiomics weighting was 0.823, whereas mean effective radiomics dominance was 0.148, with a modest case-wise association (\r{ho} = 0.290). The gated image term retained substantially stronger discriminative ranking information than the direct radiomics term. The same structural-to-effective discrepancy was observed in exploratory external evaluation. Branch-targeted permutation, integrated-gradient, and Shapley-style analyses further identified radiomics descriptors influencing the direct radiomics term. Because radiomics also generates the gate, the gated image term remains radiomics-dependent, so additive branch contribution should not be interpreted as total input influence. These findings show that structural gate weighting and decision-level branch contribution represent distinct aspects of gated feature fusion and should be interpreted separately.

Image and Video Processing.title: Beyond Discrimination: Evaluating Probability Calibration in Radiomics-Image Fusion for Renal Cell Carcinoma Classification
Image and Video Processing.summary: Reliable probability estimates are important for the clinical interpretation of machine-learning classifiers, yet radiomics--image fusion models for renal cell carcinoma (RCC) are commonly evaluated primarily by discrimination. Using 396 patients from the KiTS23 dataset, we evaluated whether adding radiomics to four image-model families improved probabilistic performance in addition to discrimination. Seventeen individual models and four probability-average ensembles were assessed using discrimination, probability calibration, and proper scoring measures. Across 12 matched image-only versus fusion comparisons, AUC and AP improved in all 12, while Brier score and negative log likelihood (NLL) improved in 11 of 12 and expected calibration error (ECE) in eight of 12. The 3D MedVAE gated-fusion model achieved the strongest overall individual-model profile. Probability averaging across concatenation, cross-attention, and gated fusion produced favourable point estimates across all five primary metrics relative to image-only models in all four families, although paired-bootstrap support was stronger for Brier score and NLL than for ECE. These findings show that radiomics--image fusion can improve probabilistic prediction quality beyond discrimination, while calibration behaviour varies across image architectures and fusion strategies. We show that our proposed probability-average ensemble models improve discrimination and calibration simultaneously across all architectures in the study.

Image and Video Processing.title: C$^2$LUE: Clinically Aligned Patient-Level Ultrasound Diagnosis via Evidence-Aware Multi-Instance Learning
Image and Video Processing.summary: Patient-level ultrasound diagnosis demands not only high predictive accuracy but also clinically aligned mitigation of asymmetric diagnostic risks. While Multi-Instance Learning (MIL) effectively models routine multi-view exams, standard aggregators often dilute heterogeneous diagnostic cues and optimize solely for global accuracy. This frequently yields undesirable sensitivity-specificity trade-offs. To bridge this gap, we propose C$^2$LUE, a novel MIL framework coupling evidence aware aggregation with risk-aligned regularization. To preserve evidence heterogeneity and prevent unimodal attention collapse, C$^2$LUE employs a multi-query cross-attention mechanism built upon a LoRA-adapted DINOv3 backbone. Multiple latent queries explicitly extract and disentangle diverse morphological patterns from the ultrasound sequence. Furthermore, to improve clinical risk alignment, we introduce a dynamic trade-off regularization objective that penalizes sensitivity-specificity imbalance during training. Rather than leaving the clinical trade-off entirely to post-hoc threshold adjustment, this objective encourages the learned score distribution toward a more balanced operating region. Extensive evaluations on patient-level, biopsy-proven thyroid and breast ultrasound datasets demonstrate that C$^2$LUE consistently outperforms prior alternatives. By uniting strong discrimination with a balanced error profile, C$^2$LUE provides a promising solution for real-world ultrasound screening and diagnosis.

Image and Video Processing.title: Frozen Site-Probe Accuracy Is Not a Standalone Harmonization Score: An Audit of Evaluation Practice for Multi-Site MRI
Image and Video Processing.summary: Image-level MRI harmonization is often evaluated with a frozen site probe, a site classifier trained on raw scans and applied unchanged to harmonized ones: a drop in its accuracy is read as removal of site effects. We audit this practice on ABIDE I (1,112 T1-weighted scans, 17 sites) with ten output sets from seven harmonization methods and controls for chance, head shape, intensity, preprocessing and target alignment. We find that this verdict depends on how the probe is trained, even among probes that classify raw scans well: across random seeds, its balanced accuracy on the same CycleGAN outputs ranges from 0.13 to 0.59 (chance: 0.06). Low frozen-probe accuracy can also arise without harmonization: a Gaussian blur, which increases the intensity distance to the target site, lowers this accuracy to chance. Moreover, where the frozen probe fails, probes trained on the harmonized scans still recover the site, even from intensity histograms alone: on HACA3 outputs, the frozen probe scores 0.25, a probe trained on those outputs 0.75, and one using only their intensity histograms 0.71. Low frozen-probe accuracy therefore does not show that site information has been removed. We recommend reporting several probes trained to convergence, probes trained on harmonized scans, and target alignment.

Image and Video Processing.title: Exploring the Latent Structure of AMD Severity Using Retinal Foundation Models
Image and Video Processing.summary: Retinal foundation models have demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of ophthalmic tasks, yet relatively little is known about how disease-related information is represented within their learned embeddings and whether this distribution influences downstream prediction performance. In this work, we use Age-related Macular Degeneration (AMD) as a case study to investigate how disease severity is represented within the embedding space of RET-CLIP, a retinal vision-language foundation model, using bilateral fundus images from the AREDS dataset, benchmarked against non-retinal encoders. We first characterize the distribution of AMD severity within the learned representation space and then evaluate how this structure influences classification performance across three clinically relevant task formulations of increasing granularity. Finally, we analyze the most influential latent dimensions combining feature attribution, statistical phenotype association, and qualitative image analyses. Our results show that RET-CLIP represents AMD severity as a continuous spectrum rather than a set of discrete categories, with healthy and advanced disease stages exhibiting clearer separation than intermediate ones. This organization was reflected in downstream performance, which decreased from a balanced accuracy of 0.844 and 0.814 for binary AMD and Late-AMD detection respectively to 0.446 for six-class grading. Furthermore, the most influential latent dimensions were statistically associated to distinct retinal phenotypes, including drusen accumulation, pigmentary alterations, and advanced retinal lesions. These findings suggest that the structure of retinal foundation-model representations influences the difficulty of clinically relevant prediction tasks and demonstrate the potential of representation-level analysis for understanding disease organization and improving interpretability.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Constructive Arboricity in Almost-Linear Time for Dense Graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The arboricity of a graph is the minimum number of forests needed to partition its edges. We present a randomized algorithm that computes the exact arboricity of a simple graph and constructs an optimal forest partition in $\min\{n^{2+o(1)},m^{4/3+o(1)}\}$ time both in expectation and with high probability, where $n$ and $m$ denote the numbers of vertices and edges. In particular, it runs in almost-linear time, $O(m^{1+o(1)})$, on dense graphs with $m=Θ(n^2)$.
  We also give the first known almost-linear-time algorithm that constructs a partition into at most one more forest than optimal.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Exact Algorithms for Distance to Unique Vertex Cover
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Horiyama et al. (AAAI 2024) studied the problem of generating graph instances that possess a unique minimum vertex cover under specific conditions. Their approach involved pre-assigning certain vertices to be part of the solution or excluding them from it. Notably, for the \textsc{Vertex Cover} problem, pre-assigning a vertex is equivalent to removing it from the graph. Horiyama et al.~focused on maintaining the size of the minimum vertex cover after these modifications. In this work, we extend their study by relaxing this constraint: our goal is to ensure a unique minimum vertex cover, even if the removal of a vertex may not incur a decrease on the size of said cover.
  Surprisingly, our relaxation introduces significant theoretical challenges. We observe that the problem is $Σ^2_P$-complete, and remains so even for planar graphs of maximum degree 5. Nevertheless, we provide a linear time algorithm for trees, which is then further leveraged to show that MU-VC is in \textsf{FPT} when parameterized by the combination of treewidth and maximum degree. Finally, we show that MU-VC is in \textsf{XP} when parameterized by clique-width while it is fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) if we add the size of the solution as part of the parameter.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: This is the full version of a paper presented in AAAI26

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Efficient Algorithms for Online Subadditive Combinatorial Allocations
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: For the online combinatorial allocation problem with subadditive valuations, Correa and Cristi (STOC 2023) proved the existence of a $6$-competitive online algorithm, improving on the previous best $O(\log\!\log m)$-competitive online algorithm due to Dütting, Kesselheim, and Lucier (FOCS 2020), where $m$ is the number of items. However, Correa and Cristi's result is existential, and it was left open whether a constant competitive ratio is attainable via an efficient online algorithm that uses a polynomial number of demand oracle queries. In this work, we answer this affirmatively, giving an expected-polynomial-time $(6 + ε)$-competitive online algorithm for any constant $ε> 0$. Our techniques also recover, in the offline setting, the $(2 + ε)$-approximation result of Feige (STOC, 2006). Finally, when the buyers' valuations are drawn from identical distributions, we exploit symmetry to obtain an improved $(60/11+ε)$-competitive algorithm. Starting with the natural configuration LP relaxation for the problem, our main technical contribution is a recursive Bundle Score Generator (BSG) that resolves item conflicts by assigning correlated scores to the items requested by each buyer. Unlike the Random Score Generator whose existence is shown by Correa and Cristi, our BSG is efficiently computable in expected polynomial time. Moreover, it satisfies a stochastic dominance property that is sufficient to recover both Feige's offline result and Correa and Cristi's online result.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Hamiltonian locality testing and certification do not achieve the Heisenberg limit
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We establish lower bounds for Hamiltonian property testing with access to the time-evolution operator but not its inverse. Each experiment may query the time-evolution operator multiple times, and distances between Hamiltonians are measured in the normalized Frobenius norm.
  In this model, we show that testing whether a Hamiltonian is $k$-local or $\varepsilon$-far from every $k$-local Hamiltonian requires $Ω(1/\varepsilon^2)$ total evolution time, matching the upper bound of Kallaugher and Liang (TQC'25). We also prove that testing whether an unknown Hamiltonian equals a target Hamiltonian or is $\varepsilon$-far from it requires $Ω(1/\varepsilon^2)$ total evolution time, matching the upper bound of Sinha and Tong (2025). These are the first lower bounds for natural problems in Hamiltonian learning and testing that rule out Heisenberg-limited scaling of $1/\varepsilon$.
  As a third result, we show that amplitude estimation to precision $\varepsilon$ requires $Ω(1/\varepsilon^2)$ total time evolution, recovering the result of Tang and Wright (QIP'26) in the continuous-time query model. All three results follow from the hardness of distinguishing the zero Hamiltonian from a suitably chosen ensemble of random Hamiltonians. We establish this hardness by adapting the continuous-time adversary method to forward Hamiltonian evolution.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Machine Unlearning for Federated Socially Fair k-Means Clustering
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Federated clustering can support applications such as patient stratification across hospitals and customer segmentation across distributed financial datasets. Responsible AI calls for fair representation of demographic groups and support for data deletion, motivated in part by rights such as the GDPR's right to erasure. These goals interact: deleting records can change the balance between groups and alter the clustering of the remaining population. We study exact machine unlearning for federated socially fair $k$-means, whose objective is to minimize the largest group-average squared distance to the nearest center. Our approach keeps separate local summaries for each group, so summaries at unaffected institutions remain valid as global fairness weights change. For two groups, we prove an initialization approximation guarantee independent of client group proportions under ideal sampling, and we show that same-seed replay reproduces retraining exactly. Reuse pays off most when a whole client withdraws: across three datasets, replay is $35.8\times$ faster than retraining for the initialization-only model and remains $2.4\times$ and $1.7\times$ faster with one and two fair-refinement rounds, which improve worst-group cost. For individual record deletions, gains are modest (about $1.06\times$), and certifying cached assignments can cost more than it saves. These results map where exact unlearning can profitably reuse computation. Code and reproducibility materials are available at https://github.com/arareddy/mufsc.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Tight asymptotic competitive ratio for the Canadian Traveller Problem on unit-weighted grids
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study the $k$-Canadian Traveller Problem (k-ctp), an online navigation problem introduced by Papadimitriou and Yannakakis in 1991. Given an undirected weighted graph $G=(V,E,ω)$ and two vertices $s,t\in V$, a traveller aims at navigating from $s$ to $t$ while minimizing the total distance travelled. However, up to $k$ edges of the graph may be blocked, and the traveller discovers that an edge is blocked only upon reaching one of its endpoints. The performance of an online algorithm for k-ctp is measured with the competitive ratio, which is the quotient between the distance actually traversed and the distance traversed by an omniscient traveller who knows all blockages in advance. A general lower bound $2k+1$ for the competitive ratio of deterministic algorithms remains valid even when the input graph is series-parallel, whereas constant competitive ratios can be achieved on restricted graph classes, such as cycles or unit-weighted outerplanar graphs. In this paper, we establish the first intermediate competitive ratio between constant and linear regimes. We prove that, on unit-weighted solid grid graphs, there exists an online algorithm with competitive ratio $O(\sqrt{k})$. This ratio is asymptotically tight and cannot be defeated, even on unit-weighted square grids. Finally, we show that both the unit-weighted and solidity assumptions are essential: going further with arbitrary edge weights (even on square grids) or non-solid unit-weighted grid structures yields a linear lower bound of $Ω(k)$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: The Upper Clique Transversal Problem: Hardness and Algorithms
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: A clique transversal in a graph is a set of vertices intersecting all maximal cliques. The problem of determining the minimum size of a clique transversal has received considerable attention in the literature. In this paper, we initiate the study of the ''upper'' variant of this parameter, the upper clique transversal number, defined as the maximum size of a minimal clique transversal. We investigate this parameter from the algorithmic and complexity points of view, with a focus on various graph classes. We show that the corresponding decision problem is NP-complete in the classes of chordal graphs, chordal bipartite graphs, cubic planar bipartite graphs, and line graphs of bipartite graphs, but solvable in linear time in the classes of split graphs, proper interval graphs, and cographs, and in polynomial time for graphs of bounded cliquewidth. We conclude the paper with a number of open questions.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: A preliminary version appeared in the proceedings of the 49th International Workshop on Graph-Theoretic Concepts in Computer Science (WG 2023)

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Simultaneous Competitive and Regret Guarantees for TCP Acknowledgment
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study simultaneous competitive and regret guarantees for TCP acknowledgment. Each acknowledgment serves all pending packets, and the objective is to minimize the total acknowledgment and waiting costs. It is well known that no deterministic online algorithm achieves a competitive ratio better than $2$. Given $k$ randomized online experts and $0<\varepsilon<1$, we construct a randomized online algorithm whose realized total cost is always at most $(2+\varepsilon)$ times the offline optimal cost $\mathrm{OPT}$ and whose expected regret against the expert with the smallest realized cost is $O(\sqrt{\mathrm{OPT}\log(k+1)}+\log(1/\varepsilon))$. The algorithm requires no advance knowledge of the number of packets or $\mathrm{OPT}$. Our algorithm controls switching costs between experts and uses the gap between the permitted competitive bound and its current cost to determine when to learn. We also prove lower bounds showing that, for $k\ge 2$, this regret bound is asymptotically optimal in $\mathrm{OPT}$, $k$, and $\varepsilon$, and that $\varepsilon>0$ is necessary for sublinear regret.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Faster and simpler traversal of 0/1-polytopes
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Recently, Merino and Mütze (FOCS'23+SICOMP'24) presented an algorithm for computing a Hamilton path on the skeleton of any 0/1-polytope ${\rm conv}(X)$, where $X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n$. The algorithm uses as a black box an algorithm for solving the classical linear optimization problem $\min\{w\cdot x\mid x\in X\}$ for some weight vector $w\in\mathbb{R}^n$. The resulting delay per visited vertex on the Hamilton path is only by a $\log n$ factor larger than the time to solve one instance of the optimization algorithm. In this paper, we make the Hamilton path algorithm simpler and faster. Namely, we obtain an amortized delay that is only by a constant factor larger than the running time of the optimization algorithm, thus removing the $\log n$ factor. As concrete results, this yields improved algorithms for generating bases and independent sets in a matroid, spanning trees, forests, matchings and maximum matchings in a graph, vertex covers, minimum vertex covers, independent sets and maximum independent sets in a bipartite graph, and antichains, maximum antichains and ideals in a poset. All of these listings correspond to Hamilton paths on the corresponding polytopes. Furthermore, we obtain an $\mathcal{O}(t_{\rm LP})$ amortized delay algorithm for the vertex enumeration problem on 0/1-polytopes $\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid Ax\leq b\}$, where $A\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and $b\in\mathbb{R}^m$, and $t_{\rm LP}$ is the time needed to solve the linear program $\min\{w\cdot x\mid Ax\leq b\}$. This improves upon the $\mathcal{O}(t_{\rm LP} \log n)$ delay algorithm of Merino and Mütze, and the previous $\mathcal{O}(t_{\rm LP}\,n)$ delay algorithm of Bussieck and Lübbecke from 1998.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Breaking Two Barriers for Dynamic Planar Reachability
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We consider the reachability problem in fully dynamic directed planar graphs: the graph undergoes edge updates (insertions and deletions) and we receive queries asking if one vertex is reachable from another. The current-best online algorithm for dynamic planar reachability spends worst-case time $\widetilde{O}(n^{2/3})$ per query/update [Subramanian, ESA '93]. This can be improved to $\widetilde{O}(n^{1/2})$ in the offline setting or when the embedding is fixed [Diks and Sankowski, ESA '07]. Our contribution is twofold:
  1. We present the first algorithm that breaks the square-root barrier for dynamic planar reachability in the offline setting, obtaining time ${O}(n^{0.49})$ per query/update. This shows that the problem is easier than answering distance queries in a dynamic undirected planar graph, for which a conditional lower bound of $n^{1/2 - o(1)}$ is known [Abboud and Dahlgaard, FOCS '16]. Notably, this lower bound applies to both online and offline algorithms.
  2. Second, in the general online setting we design a randomized data structure with amortized update and query time ${O}(n^{0.664})$. This is the first improvement upon the exponent $2/3$ in over three decades.
  The main engine behind our theorems is a new sparsification framework aimed at maintaining information about reachability. Specifically, we study digraphs through the lens of VC dimensionality of certain set systems. First, we design sparse reachability emulators for planar digraphs that preserve the VC dimension. Second, we utilize orderings with a low ``stabbing number'' [Chazelle and Welzl, Discrete Comput. Geom. '89] to compute subquadratic reachability emulators in subquadratic time whenever the VC dimension is bounded.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Deterministic Girth Approximation in Weighted Undirected Graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We give deterministic algorithms for approximating the girth~$g$ of an undirected graph with $n$ vertices, $m$ edges, and nonnegative real edge lengths. For every integer $k\geq2$, our algorithm returns a cycle of length at most $\frac{2k}{3}g$ in $O((m+n^{1+2/k})k\log n)$ worst-case time. For every constant~$k$, this matches the stretch and the expected running time of the randomized algorithms of Kadria, Roditty, Sidford, Vassilevska Williams, and Zwick [SODA'23, SICOMP'26] and Kadria, Roditty, and Vassilevska Williams [ESA'26]. In general, it loses only a factor of $O(\min\{k,\log n\})$ in the term that depends on~$m$. The best previous deterministic trade-off, of Kadria, Roditty, Sidford, Vassilevska Williams, and Zwick [SODA'22], has stretch~$k$ instead of $\frac{2k}{3}$ at the same exponent (for even~$k$) and requires integer edge lengths. In particular, for $k=3$ we obtain a deterministic $2$-approximation in $O((m+n^{5/3})\log n)$ time for real edge lengths, whereas the deterministic algorithm of Ducoffe [SIDMA'21] for real lengths has stretch $2+\varepsilon$.
  Our main technical idea is that a deterministic construction of the Thorup--Zwick hierarchy used by these algorithms may stop exploring as soon as it finds a cycle: the approximation analysis only needs clusters truncated at half the best cycle certificate found, so balls stopped in this way need not be hit. Together with a degree-weighted selection rule, this bounds the work of each level by its number of edges and stored ball entries. More generally, a ball need not be hit whenever the analysis only uses clusters up to a radius bounded by a certificate that the algorithm has already found.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: An ETH-based quasipolynomial lower bound for Dualization
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Dualizing monotone Boolean functions (or equivalently, enumerating minimal transversals in hypergraphs) is a long-standing problem whose output-polynomial-time solvability remains open. While various special cases have been extensively studied, the state-of-the-art algorithm for the general case, due to Fredman and Khachiyan, runs in quasipolynomial time. This paper presents a subexponential-time reduction from \textsc{3SAT} to the complement of \textsc{Dual}: Given a 3CNF formula with $n$ variables, the reduction constructs hypergraphs $H$ and $L$ of total size $2^{O(n^{2/3}(\log n)^{1/3})}$ such that $L \subseteq Tr(H)$ and the formula is satisfiable if and only if $L\neq Tr(H)$, where $Tr(H)$ is the set of minimal transversals of $H$. As a consequence of this reduction, assuming the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), neither \textsc{Dual} nor \textsc{Dualization} admits an algorithm running in $N^{o(\sqrt{\log N/\log\log N})}$ time, where $N$ is the input size for \textsc{Dual} and the combined input and output size for \textsc{Dualization}. In particular, \textsc{Dualization} cannot be solved in output-polynomial time under ETH.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: The directed temporal exploration problem
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study the temporal exploration problem on temporal digraphs. We prove that a lifetime of $O(n^2)$ suffices to guarantee the existence of a temporal exploration on always-unilateral temporal digraphs. We complement this with a $Ω(n^2)$ lower bound, even in the case where each snapshot has maximum undirected degree 2; for always-strong temporal digraphs, the lower bound still holds even if the maximum undirected degree is 3. This stands in stark contrast with the undirected setting.
  For the large minimum degree setting, we show that a lifetime of $4n/3 - 1$ is sufficient and necessary for guaranteeing the existence of a temporal exploration on temporal digraphs where each snapshot is semicomplete. For always-strong temporal digraphs where each snapshot has minimum undirected degree at least $n - c - 1$, we prove that a lifetime of $O(cn)$ guarantees the existence of a temporal exploration, and we also prove that this is asymptotically tight.
  From a computational perspective, our results for temporal semicomplete digraphs also yield a polynomial-time, factor-$4/3$ algorithm for deciding if a temporal semicomplete digraph admits a temporal exploration within the first $\ell$ snapshots. We complement this showing that no polynomial-time, factor-$(4/3 - ε)$ approximation algorithm exists, even if every snapshot is a tournament, unless P$=$NP.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Breaking the 1/3 Barrier for constrained $\boldsymbol{k}$-Submodular Maximization: A Proportional Top-2 Randomized Framework
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: $k$-submodularity generalizes submodularity by allowing each selected element to be assigned one of $k$ labels. We study the maximization of a non-monotone $k$-submodular function, where $k\ge2$, under matroid and knapsack constraints. We develop a proportional top-2 randomized framework that achieves an approximation ratio of $\sqrt2-1\approx0.4142$ under either constraint, breaking the previous $1/3$ barrier. Once an element is selected, its label is chosen from the two labels with the largest marginal gains, with probabilities proportional to their positive parts. The analysis separates replacement, pure-addition, and residual-deletion losses, and proves a sharp local loss certificate for this rule. We then give a Bellman analysis using the same local certificate. It gives a $1/2$-approximation under a cardinality constraint and strengthens the knapsack guarantee to $1/2$ without changing the algorithm. The $1/2$ guarantees are oracle-optimal for $k=2$ and asymptotically tight as $k\to\infty$. The value-oracle complexities are $O(Bnk)$ for cardinality, where $B$ is the cardinality bound, $O(n^2k)$ for matroid, and $O(n^3k^2)$ for knapsack.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Polynomial directed treewidth forces a large bramble with congestion two
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Brambles of constant congestion in directed graphs have interesting structural and algorithmic applications, and it is desirable to find the smallest function $f_c(k)$ such that if a digraph has directed treewidth at least $f_c(k)$, then it contains a bramble of size at least $k$ and congestion at most $c$. By the Directed Grid Theorem of Kawarabayashi and Kreutzer [STOC 2015], such a function $f_c(k)$ exists for every value $c \geq 2$ of the congestion. However, even using the recent improvements due to Hatzel et al. [FOCS 2024], the resulting function is a power tower of height $22$. Recently, Masařík et al. [SIAM J. Discrete Math. 2022] proved that, for congestion $8$, the function $f_8(k)$ can be made polynomial; more precisely, they showed that $f_8(k) = \mathcal{O}(k^{48} \cdot \log^{13} k)$. They asked whether it is possible to decrease the congestion, ideally to $2$, even at the cost of a higher polynomial function. In this work we answer their question affirmatively with the best possible value of the congestion, by proving that $f_2(k) = \mathcal{O}(k^{96}\cdot \log^{23} k)$. We also obtain smaller polynomials for higher congestion, namely $f_4(k) = \mathcal{O}(k^{72} \cdot \log^{21} k)$ and $f_6(k) = \mathcal{O}(k^{66} \cdot \log^{18} k)$. Our results are inspired by the proof for congestion $8$, which we improve by introducing walkages. Walkages allow us to avoid technicalities of the original proof by translating ideas due to Reed and Wood [Eur. J. Comb. 2012] that work for undirected graphs to the directed setting. Our proofs are constructive and naturally yield polynomial-time algorithms to find the brambles assuming a certificate for large directed treewidth is given. Moreover, we discuss algorithmic applications of our results for the Directed Disjoint Paths with Congestion problem, and to half-integral packings of subgraphs with large directed treewidth.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Deterministic Linear-Time Modular Subset Sum
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We give a deterministic $O(m)$-time algorithm for exact modular subset sum over every modulus $m$. The input gives distinct residues and their multiplicities. The algorithm reports all reachable residues and answers one target query. It returns a witness when the target is reachable. The algorithm uses $O(m)$ auxiliary words on an arithmetic word-RAM. This improves Potępa's deterministic $O(m\log m\,α(m))$-time bound under the same input convention. The running time matches the cost of explicitly reporting all $m$ reachability bits.
  We represent reachable residues as runs along cycles of repeated addition. Newly reached residues pay for scans of partial runs. We process prime factors in increasing order so that cycle rebuilding takes linear time. A theorem on subset sums of distinct units limits the number of adaptive boundary batches to $O(m^{3/4})$. Radix sorting their $O(m)$ total keys also takes $O(m)$ time.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Classical and Quantum Heuristics for the Binary Paint Shop Problem
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The Binary Paint Shop Problem (BPSP) is an $\mathsf{APX}$-hard optimisation problem arising in automotive manufacturing: given a sequence of $2n$ cars, comprising $n$ distinct models each appearing twice, the task is to decide which of two colours to paint each car so that the two occurrences of each model are painted differently, while minimising consecutive colour swaps. Performance is measured by the paint swap ratio -- the average number of colour changes per car -- which directly affects production efficiency and cost. Prior work showed that the Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm (QAOA) at depth $p=7$ achieves a ratio of $0.393$, outperforming the then-best-known classical heuristic, Recursive Greedy, with a proven asymptotic expected ratio of $0.4$ [Phys. Rev. A 104, 012403 (2021)]. More recently, the Recursive Star Greedy (RSG) heuristic was proposed with a conjectured expected ratio of $0.361$. Here, we formally reduce BPSP to weighted MaxCut, yielding an exact Ising formulation, and benchmark two state-of-the-art low-depth QAOA variants -- eXpressive QAOA and Recursive QAOA -- at $p=1$ (denoted XQAOA$_1$ and RQAOA$_1$) against four classical BPSP heuristics. Across instances ranging from $2^7$ to $2^{12}$ cars, XQAOA$_1$ achieves an average paint-swap ratio of $0.357$; in our instance-wise benchmarks, it outperforms RQAOA$_1$ on almost all instances and each of the four classical baselines, including RSG, on every instance. Surprisingly, RQAOA$_1$ deteriorates with problem size despite employing provably near-optimal QAOA$_1$ parameters at each recursive step, eventually falling behind RSG at the largest sizes. To our knowledge, this is the first report of size-dependent performance degradation of RQAOA$_1$ at scale. In contrast, XQAOA$_1$ remains stable across all tested sizes, with no evidence of size-dependent degradation.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 32 pages, 3 figures. Final revised version accepted for publication in Physical Review Applied

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Checking and producing word attractors
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The article focuses on word (or string) attractors, which are sets of positions related to the text compression efficiency of the underlying word. The article presents two combinatorial algorithms based on Suffix automata or Directed Acyclic Word Graphs. The first algorithm decides in linear time whether a set of positions on the word is an attractor of the word. The second algorithm generates an attractor for a given word in a greedy manner. Although the problem of generating a smallest attractor is NP-hard, {the algorithm is efficient and produces very small attractors and even the smallest ones for several well-known infinite families of words.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Minimizing fuzzy Kripke models over residuated lattices
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Model minimization is a fundamental problem in formal methods, as smaller models can substantially reduce the complexity of model analysis and reasoning while preserving relevant semantic properties. This work studies the minimization of finite fuzzy Kripke models over residuated lattices while preserving global or local assertions in fuzzy modal logics, which are either fuzzy propositional dynamic logic or a restriction thereof, optionally enriched with nominals, converse modalities, and/or the universal program constructor. We prove that, whenever the multiplication operator of the underlying residuated lattice is right-continuous, the quotient model induced by the greatest fuzzy auto-bisimulation is a minimal reduction preserving global assertions. If the underlying fuzzy modal logic includes the universal program constructor, this quotient model is also a minimal reduction preserving local assertions and a minimal fuzzy Kripke model bisimilar to the original model. In the case where the universal program constructor is absent and the multiplication operator is additionally strictly monotone with respect to~1, we present the first algorithm for constructing a minimal reduction preserving local assertions; the resulting model is also a minimal bisimilar model.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Dynamic Matching with Abandonment: Optimal Guarantees via Static Priority Policies
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study stochastic dynamic matching with abandonment, a fundamental model in which agents of different types arrive over time, may abandon the market while waiting, and can be matched in pairs for rewards that depend on their types. No online policy can guarantee more than $0.5$ of the omniscient benchmark, which knows all arrival and departure times. Whether this guarantee is achievable has been a central open problem, even in special cases. We resolve this problem by showing that, on every instance, a simple static priority policy, which is computable in polynomial time, earns at least $0.5$ of the omniscient benchmark. This establishes that the optimal competitive ratio is exactly $0.5$, improving the previous best guarantee of 0.192 for the general model [Li et al. 2026; Collina et al. 2020]
  Our analysis rests on a key stochastic result, which is a new lower bound on the probability that some agent from a given set of types is available. Building on this bound, we develop two approaches: a primal approach that reads the priorities from an optimal solution of a novel linear program, and a dual approach that assigns a ``value'' to each type, and prioritizes matches with high ``surplus'' (reward minus value of involved agents). These values are the unique solution of a fixed-point equation derived from linear programming duality. We also show that the two approaches are closely connected.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Subset Sum and Integer Programming Feasibility Test in Near-Optimal Time
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Given an integer $t$ and a set of integers in $[N]$, Subset Sum asks whether there exists a subset that sums to $t$. A long open problem is whether Subset Sum can be solved in $O(N)$ time. We show that Subset Sum can be solved in $O(N^{1 + \varepsilon})$ time where $\varepsilon > 0$ is an arbitrarily small constant. Our result also generalizes to multi-sets in multi-dimension. That is, for any fixed $d$ and $\varepsilon >0$, the $d$-dimensional subset sum can be solved in $O(n + N^{d + \varepsilon})$ time. As an application, for any fixed $d$ and $\varepsilon$, feasibility test of integer programming with $d$ constraints can be done in $O(N^{d+\varepsilon} \mathrm{poly}(\ell_{\mathrm{in}}))$ time, where $N$ is the maximum absolute value in the constraint matrix and $\ell_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the input size.
  Although the algorithm is quite involved, its high-level idea is clear. It is already known that when the input set is dense and $t$ lies in the interior of the zonotope, then Subset Sum is easy to solve [Galil-Margalit '91, Bringmann-Wellnitz '21, Chen-Hu-Mao-Zhang '26]. Our key observation is that a sparse input can exhibit a dense structure when lifted to higher dimension. We show that such a lifting can be done efficiently. After lifting, the interior of the zonotope is easy to tackle, and one only needs to deal with the thin area near the boundary of the zonotope. Then we show that the boundary area can be decomposed into subproblems and solved recursively, and that there cannot be too many recursion levels since each level of recursive reduces the volume of the area significantly.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Conditional Indexing Lower Bounds and Normalization Boundaries for Elastic Subsequence Matching
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study static indexes for exact subsequence matching over all equal-length windows of a time series. Under deterministic SETH, for every fixed $β\ge1$ and $δ\in(0,1)$, we exclude $O(N^β)$ preprocessing together with $O(N^{1-δ})$ worst-case query time on domains containing the reduction's polylogarithmic query lengths. The bounded-error counterpart assumes randomized SETH. The results cover specified warping, bottleneck, edit, subsequence, local-alignment, and complexity-adjusted scores. Their reductions share a data-independent query interface but require different arguments for all-window soundness. We give complete representative proofs for the distinct mechanisms and state the changes needed by related scores. For soft-DTW, integer scaling yields an exact Boolean-predicate reduction in Word-RAM; a model with exact transcendental primitives requires a separate assumption. For independent window-wise Z-normalization, balanced coordinate gadgets and shifted-window moment bounds yield exact lower bounds for squared-cost DTW and discrete Fréchet distance. We give finite-word comparisons and a specified length-dependent rounding rule preserving these gaps. Raw and normalized discrete Fréchet constructions also exclude feasible-solution approximation within any fixed factor below two. Finally, we prove conditional signal-attenuation bounds for normalized anchor constructions and a fast index under the all-window common-mean promise.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Directed Global Minimum Cut in Almost-Linear Time
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We give a randomized reduction from global minimum cut in a directed graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ weighted edges to maximum-flow computations on graphs of total size $\widetilde{O}(m)$. For polynomially bounded integral weights, this yields the first almost-linear $m^{1+o(1)}$-time algorithm [vdBCK+23], improving the previous $m^{1+o(1)}\min\{\sqrt{n},n/m^{1/3}\}$ bound [CLN+22].
  Previous work reduced finding the minimum cut to constructing a 1-respecting arborescence, a directed spanning tree with exactly one edge crossing a minimum cut [CLN+22]. They then construct such a tree by sampling from a $(1+ε)$-approximate arborescence packing, which currently requires superlinear time. Our algorithm sidesteps constructing the packing entirely and relies on a novel iterative arborescence sampling procedure. We show that, after $O(\log n)$ rounds of sampling, our final arborescence 1-respects the minimum cut with constant probability.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Improved classical optimization of fermionic Hamiltonians beyond Gaussian states
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We give a polynomial-time randomized classical algorithm that approximates the largest eigenvalue $λ_{\max}$ of a traceless quartic fermionic Hamiltonian $H$ on $n$ modes. The algorithm achieves energy at least $λ_{\max}/O(\sqrt n)$ and outputs either a fermionic Gaussian state or a polynomially sparse state in the Fock basis. This is achieved through a new upper bound on $λ_{\max}$ in terms of the maximum energy of a Gaussian state and $\sqrt{2^{-n}\operatorname{Tr}(H^2)}$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Separable convex optimization over indegree polytopes
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study separable discrete convex optimization over indegree vectors of orientations of an undirected graph, focusing on the effect of imposing acyclicity. Since the extreme points of the indegree polytope are precisely the indegree vectors of acyclic orientations, this amounts to comparing optimization over its integer points with optimization over its extreme points. Over all orientations, minimizing a vertex-separable discrete convex objective is strongly polynomial-time solvable by minimum-cost flow. Over acyclic orientations, for every fixed discrete convex function shared by all vertices, we obtain a dichotomy: if the function is linear on the positive integers, the problem is solvable in linear time; otherwise exact optimization is NP-hard on connected simple graphs, and APX-hard when the function is non-negative. We also give strongly polynomial-time constant-factor approximation algorithms for broad classes of convex and concave objectives. For the $p$-power sum of indegrees, this yields a $2^p$-approximation for every fixed integer $p\geq1$, while the problem is APX-complete for every fixed integer $p\geq2$; if $p$ is part of the input, no deterministic polynomial-time $2^{p^{1-\varepsilon}}$-approximation exists for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$ unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$. We further give an exact $O(2^{|V|}|V|+\operatorname{poly}(|V|,|E|))$-time dynamic program for general separable objectives, with a matching lower bound in the exponent under the Exponential Time Hypothesis. Finally, decreasingly minimal and increasingly maximal acyclic orientations need not coincide and are both NP-hard, while minimizing the maximum weighted indegree over acyclic orientations remains strongly polynomial-time solvable.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: The Sample Complexity of Multicalibration with an ERM Oracle
